name: FairVote: ranked-choice voting and proportional representation (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the people in the US places that adopt ranked-choice voting or proportional representation.
summary: FairVote researches and campaigns for ranked-choice voting and proportional representation in the United States ($6.4 million in 2024). A dollar to FairVote is counted as doing what the average dollar behind each movement did in 2016-2025: the ranked-choice movement (about $19 million a year, ballot campaigns included) put about 1.4 million more Americans a year under ranked ballots for some of their offices, and the proportional-representation movement (about $3.4 million a year) about 103,000 a year under proportional representation, each valued as a small share (2% and 5%) of the income democracy brings (Acemoglu et al. 2019), building over 25 years, brought forward by the years a win counts and repealed at 3% a year; ranked-choice voting gives about four fifths of the result. With its next dollar at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the average that comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars. The biggest uncertainty is whether a voting method changes how well people are governed at all, a judgment with no study of its size; both branches are discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Income gained per person-year once the effect is fully built, ln(consumption) (RCV branch)
rows.explainer: Ranked-choice voting's share (@democracy.rcv_gain_share, 2%, 0.3% to 6%) of the long-run income gain of becoming a democracy (@democracy.democratization_gdp_gain, 21%): the family's rule for a reform within a democracy. The build-up is in rcv_discounted_years.

rows.label: Years from the win until ranked ballots are first used
rows.explainer: The shared figure: about a year and a half (1 to 3).

rows.label: Discount for the wait (RCV branch)
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discount rate plus repeal hazard (RCV branch)
rows.explainer: The shared rate plus the shared yearly chance a won electoral reform is repealed or banned (@democracy.electoral_reform_repeal_rate, 3%, its anchor the record of US ranked-choice repeals and state bans): repeal is a separate question from the years counted (the family's rule).

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years a won reform counts (RCV branch, its ramp brought forward)
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + rcv_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + rcv_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + rcv_rate) * ln(1 + rcv_rate) * ramp_years) * rcv_wait_discount
rows.explainer: The family's shifted ramp: the effect builds over ramp_years from first use, and bringing the reform forward by years_of_impact moves the whole ramp earlier; present value at the shared rate plus the repeal hazard, times the wait.

rows.label: Units of value per year of the movement's work (RCV branch, before adjustments)
rows.explainer: People newly covered × the income gained × the value of a log point × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.explainer: The shared figure: the movement's 2016-2025 record, about {{row:pr_people}} people a year (85,000 to 115,000), Portland, Oregon's 2022 reform most of it.

rows.explainer: Proportional representation's share (@democracy.pr_gain_share, 5%, 1% to 15%) of the democratization gain.

rows.label: Share of a full switch that the places counted get, RCV branch
rows.explainer: The shared figures, about 44%: the local part (@democracy.rcv_local_coverage, 68%) × the share of a full switch a city's own elections bring (@democracy.local_offices_weight, 50%), as in the PR branch, plus the state and federal part (@democracy.rcv_state_federal_coverage, 10%); weighted by the people added: New York City uses ranked ballots for its primaries and special elections, Maine for primaries and federal races, Hawaii only for special elections, cities for their own offices (@democracy.local_offices_weight).

rows.label: Share of a full switch that the places counted get, PR branch
rows.explainer: The shared figures: the adopting places use proportional representation for about 82% of their own elections (Portland, Oregon its whole council, Arlington County only its board), and a city's own elections are about half of a full switch (@democracy.local_offices_weight): about 41%.

rows.label: FairVote's share of the ranked-choice movement's resources
rows.explainer: FairVote's 2024 spending on single-winner ranked-choice voting (about $5.1 million) over the whole movement's average yearly spending in 2016-2025 (@democracy.us_rcv_movement_resources_per_year, $19 million, ballot campaigns and FairVote included; Convention 2): about {{row:rcv_attribution_share_shared}}. Its 2024 spending is above its 2016-2024 average ($4.1 million a year nominal, $4.7 million in 2024 prices), so this is the share a 2024 year of its work would be of an average movement year; the result per dollar is the movement's wins per dollar it spent, whatever FairVote's own spending.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.label: Share of credit used: FairVote's share of the ranked-choice movement's resources
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: FairVote's share of the proportional-representation movement's resources
rows.explainer: FairVote's 2024 spending on proportional representation (about $1.3 million) over the whole movement's average yearly spending in 2016-2025 (@democracy.us_pr_movement_resources_per_year, $3.4 million, FairVote and Protect Democracy included; Convention 2): about {{row:pr_attribution_share_shared}}. As in the RCV branch, a 2024 year of its work against an average movement year, so the result per dollar is the movement's wins per dollar it spent.
